title: Rice Fertilizer Schedule by Target Yield, in Bags per Hectare
metaTitle: Rice Fertilizer Schedule: Bags per Hectare by Target Yield
metaDescription: A rice fertilizer schedule for palay with no soil test: the bags per hectare and the day of each dose for 3 to 8 tons, by variety maturity, from PhilRice.
excerpt: A rice fertilizer schedule tells you what to apply, how many 50 kg bags per hectare, and on which day. The plan below is PhilRice's general recommendation for fields with no soil test. Pick the table for your target yield and the column for your variety's maturity. Then count the days from transplanting (DAT) or sowing (DAS).

heroImage.alt: A farmer broadcasting fertilizer by hand over a young green paddy, one dose in a rice fertilizer schedule
heroImage.credit: Soumya B, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
A general plan is a starting point, not a soil test. It assumes an average irrigated lowland field. Your own soil may hold more of one nutrient and less of another. So let a [leaf color chart](/blog/leaf-color-chart-rice) adjust the urea, and test the soil before next season.

Every bag here is a 50 kg bag, and every rate is per hectare. For a smaller lot, multiply by its size in hectares. A quarter hectare takes a quarter of each number.
Choose your target yield and maturity group

IRRI's Rice Knowledge Bank explains that the yield you aim for sets how much nutrient the crop must take up. So pick a target you have reached before on the same field, not the best harvest you have heard about. Then check the seed bag for the variety's days to maturity, or look it up in our [rice varieties](/rice-varieties) finder.

PhilRice sets three targets for inbred rice: 3 to 4, 5 to 6 and 7 to 8 tons per hectare. Hybrid rice gets its own plan for 6 to 7 tons. Each target then splits by maturity into 100 to 110 days, 111 to 120 days and 121 to 130 days. Longer varieties get their top dressings later, because they reach tillering and panicle initiation later.
Organic matter and the seedbed come first

The schedule starts before transplanting. Return the straw from your last crop, about one ton for every ton of target yield. Plow it in 30 days before transplanting so it has time to rot. Then, two weeks before transplanting, spread 10 bags of chicken manure or vermicompost and mix it into the mud.

blocks.text: Add zinc only where the soil lacks it. PalayCheck describes the sign: dusty brown spots on the upper leaves of stunted plants, 2 to 4 weeks after transplanting. For a mild shortage, it puts 0.5 kg of zinc sulfate on a 400 square meter seedbed. A severe one gets 2 kg. Our page on [micronutrients for rice](/blog/micronutrients-for-rice) covers zinc in full.
Rice fertilizer schedule for 3 to 4 tons per hectare
This is the lightest plan, with one basal dose and one top dressing, for fields that usually give 60 to 80 cavans of 50 kg.

blocks.text: How to apply each dose

items: Mix the basal dose into the mud during the final harrowing or by 14 DAT, so it sits where the young roots grow.
Keep the first dose light on nitrogen. PalayCheck puts only about 30 percent of the season's nitrogen in the first application.
Top dress into a shallow 2 to 3 cm of water, and close the outlets so the fertilizer stays in your paddy.
Spread in the afternoon, after 3 PM, because cooler air means less nitrogen lost as gas.
If you practice [alternate wetting and drying](/blog/alternate-wetting-and-drying), pause it on fertilizer days.

blocks.title: Why some PhilRice lists show fewer bags
blocks.text: PhilRice's 2022 Abonong Swak news release prints the same 5 to 6 ton plan, but its other two are lighter. Its 3 to 4 ton plan uses 1 bag of 14 14 14. Its 7 to 8 ton plan uses 2 bags of 14 14 14 and half a bag of potash. It also dates the manure at 14 days after transplanting instead of before. Both are general plans, so treat the gap as one more reason to test your soil. Our page on [bags of fertilizer per hectare](/blog/bags-of-fertilizer-per-hectare) compares them with the Nueva Ecija quick guide.
Adjust the schedule with a leaf color chart and NPK Plus

The urea rows are the part most worth adjusting. From 14 DAT, read a leaf color chart every 7 days. If 6 or more of 10 leaves read below the critical value, the crop needs nitrogen, even if the schedule says wait. If the leaves stay dark green, you can hold a dose and save the bag.

Before you buy, run your plan through [NPK Plus](/features/npk-plus-calculator), the fertilizer calculator in anee.io. Pick palay and your bags, and it adds up the nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium per hectare. Then it holds them against the usual rate for rice. If something comes out short or too much, ask Anee, the smart farm technician, what to change.

Once the plan is set, put it on your [cropping calendar](/features/cropping-calendar). In anee.io, every dose gets its date from each lot's own transplanting or sowing day. A lot planted a week late gets its urea a week late too.

blocks.text: Questions about the rice fertilizer schedule

items.q: What is the fertilizer schedule for 5 to 6 tons of palay?
items.a: PhilRice's general plan uses 2 bags of 14 14 14 or 16 20 0 per hectare by 14 DAT. Then comes 1 bag of urea between 18 and 31 DAT. The last dose, 1 bag of urea with half a bag of 0 0 60, lands between 28 and 40 DAT. The exact days follow your variety's maturity.

items.q: Can I use this schedule for direct seeded rice?
items.a: Yes. Use the DAS dates in brackets. Direct seeded rice gets its top dressings later in the count, because the days start at sowing instead of transplanting.

items.q: Do I really need the straw and manure?
items.a: The plan counts on them to supply part of the nutrients and to build the soil. Without them, the bags alone may fall short of the target, so watch the leaf color chart closely.

items.q: How do I scale the schedule down for a small lot?
items.a: Multiply by the area in hectares. On the 5 to 6 ton plan, 2,500 square meters takes half a bag of 14 14 14 at basal. Each top dressing then takes a quarter bag of urea, plus about 6 kg of 0 0 60 with the second.
